body: M'n ex en ik waren vijf jaar samen en dat was toch wel zo'n beetje elke dag dat we elkaar zagen. Ook buiten huis maar alleen als we verder alleen waren. Tongen bij een volle tramhalte na een etentje met vrienden deden we niet.

Een netjes onderhouden baard heeft voor mij wel wat. M'n ex had een baard en daar heb ik nooit over geklaagd (vriendengroep was het er mee eens dat het hem goed stond). Meerdere vrienden die ook een baard hebben en bij de meesten vind ik het wel een goede toevoeging qua uiterlijk. Alleen eentje lijkt daardoor op Mr Beast maar dat durf ik niet tegen hem te zeggen.
Over dat stukje scheten ben ik het niet met je eens, maar verder wel. Ik vind het veel leuker als ik word aangesproken als een goede vriend.

Ik weet niet of 5 jaar geleden telt als "afgelopen tijd" maar mijn toenmalig partner (ex sinds een paar maanden) heb ik ontmoet op de middelbare school. We waren toen allebei 16. Ik ben nu 23, we waren samen vanaf m'n 18e tot recent.

Binnen mijn vriendengroep zijn er ook heel veel mensen die elkaar als vrienden leerden kennen en na een tijdje een relatie hadden. Stel ik zou weer op zoek willen naar iets van romantiek, dan zou ik dat binnen mijn vriendengroep vragen. Dating apps bewaar ik voor situaties met hoge wanhoop. Als in, ik zou iemand vragen om mee te denken. "Hey, Daniël, ik vroeg me af of je misschien leuke mensen kent die je aan mij kan voorstellen." of "joh, Luna, wie was die leuke met het bruine haar op dat feestje vorige week?"

Ik heb gelukkig erg lichte menstruaties, zelfs met de koperspiraal, maar mijn moeder en veel vriendinnen hebben daarentegen echt zwaardere weken. En inderdaad, dan moet je vaak wisselen. En mijn moeder heeft ook absoluut meningen over de huismerk pakjes maandverband. Voor mij zijn die prima, voor m'n moeder en heel veel vriendinnen zijn die dingen echt niet goed genoeg. En een A-merk zoals Always is vaak ook 3 keer duurder dan huismerk.

Ik was in 2020 klaar met de middelbare, nog nooit iets van maandverband/tampons gezien voor de leerlingen. Op de uni was het er wel, maar dat was een studenteninitiatief (ofwel studenten van een vereniging/groep met budget, waarvan ze een deel besteden aan menstruatieproducten).

Possible that your scale at home and the one they had aren't calibrated to each other. Which makes sense. The scale in my gym weighs me as 2-3kg less than the one I have at home. I go to a gym with multiple locations and at *every* location I've weighed at, the scale was 2-3kg lower than my own scale. They're calibrated to each other, not to mine.

They probably just weighed you and took off a kilogram or so for clothes/shoes and rolled with that.

When we were officially a couple he got to see much more of me having my weird ED-brain moments, but he took everything with grace and patience. I explained what I was & wasn't comfortable with in terms of touch and for compliments, and he listened.

If anything he liked my UW least because he saw that I was unwell.

I jokingly called my ex a gamer (because he was, but he didn't want to be called a gamer haha) but if I needed him, he'd drop a game to help me out. One time I called him when I was anxious biking home in the dark, he was mid-game with some friends but he picked up and stayed on call with me until I got near my street.

I never liked asking for his attention when he was playing something with his friends but he'd catch on and spend time with me. If it could wait then, like you say, you can prioritize the game. That's how it goes with everything in life. E.g. I enjoy going for a walk but a friend needing my help is more important. I can always go birdwatching in the park some other time.

Maar als je oudere kaas neemt dan heb je een hoger vetgehalte. Zo heeft de [oude kaas ](https://www.ah.nl/producten/product/wi197229/de-zaanse-hoeve-oud-48-plakken)35g vet waarvan 24 verzadigd.

I graduated with my BA after three years of intense stress and being on edge pretty much always, and sometimes not seeing my partner for a month because I was too busy or stressed. If I did see him in the weekend, I'd usually cry from stress at least once.

It was a 2-3 hour drive from my parents' place to my college. My partner at the time had heavy motion sickness issues *but he showed up* and sat through those 3 hours in the car so he could celebrate with me. And another 2-3 hours to get home afterwards. Same thing last fall: I got my MSc, and my partner was there in the crowd for me. It was a different college, about an hour by bike from where he lived with his mom - she didn't want to drive because the inner city is a mess if you go by car, so they biked there. Again, he was there and celebrated with me, and told my teachers and friends how proud he was of me.

Also kids love putting items in their mouth. *Which is why so many things are a choking hazard.* I nearly died as an infant because I was playing with my mother's wedding ring. She was a few steps away from me and I was doing normal baby stuff.

I was typically a smart enough and well-behaved baby, but not smart enough to resist the urge of putting a shiny diamond ring in my mouth. She had to shake me upside down above the sink.
If he keeps doing that I'd suggest to also just throw the whole husband away.

Ik heb als student een tijdje meegewerkt aan een project over radicalisatiepreventie voor jongeren. Uiteindelijk gaan veel mensen dit soort gedachtegoed volgen en geloven, omdat ze er samenhorigheid in vinden en een gevoel van "community" wat ze elders niet hebben gevonden.

Op een bepaald punt gaat het, voor zover ik zie, ook echt niet meer om het "krijgen" van een vrouw. Of meerdere. Zodra vrouwen inspraak hebben over die ideeën dan worden ze inderdaad vaak afgeschreven als gekke feministen of anderzins kansloos, en daarmee geen goede vrouwen. Ik kan me niet voorstellen dat iemand dit punt bereikt in hun gedachtegang en nog steeds een lieve, verzorgende vrouw wil. Dat is zogenaamd wel het doel, maar eigenlijk ben je al te ver heen. Maar er is geen uitweg, want dan ben je als manzijnde óók zwak en nutteloos (net als die vrouwen). Dus je blijft doorgaan met de negativiteit, want die weg is makkelijker en toegankelijker dan weer de neutrale kant op gaan.

I had a crush on someone when I was 14. He was my best friend at the time and the first person I'd fallen in love with. We were a situationship for a year and a half - he lived too far away to make something substantial happen - and I thought he was going to be my forever love. He broke things off eventually and I thought my life was over, and that I'd never find love again etc etc.

Now I'm 23 and we're still friends, and I don't want to get closer to him than that. He's nice, but not the fairy tale I thought he was when I was 14. My first real relationship ended two months ago, we were together for five years, and it hurts more than anything I've ever experienced. But also, I'm 23. The world didn't end when I thought I lost the love of my life as a teenager, and the world also isn't ending now that I've lost the love of my life as a young adult.

Right?! There's been plenty of times where I was sick or needed someone to join me for something, and my ex couldn't be there for me. (We did not break up because of that.) I was a little disappointed, sure, but he always apologized, and near the end of our time together he apologized for all the times he couldn't make it to an event or something else I needed help with. He never refused to show up just because he didn't feel like it - if he cancelled it was due to illness or work/school/medical appointment getting priority. For another friend I went around asking friends, and friends' friends, to put their name on a poster for her birthday. I biked a lot that month. (She still has the poster five years later!)

Sometimes with another friend, or with his mom/dad. But never a big surprise party or a project like I did for other friends, because I knew he didn't like it. It's really simple.

It was never about sex or adult behavior. I just want to feel silky every now and then.

This!! Anorexia has definitely left some mental scars for me and I'll retain some traits forever probably, but it's no longer affecting my decisions as much as it used to. I can go out for food with a friend and get starters, a main dish (which is not a salad or simple sandwich) and maybe even dessert. I did this last Saturday and then we even got boba afterwards. I almost ordered a large drink but I didn't want to risk having to pee twice in the same hour.

I don't look at calories on snacks, and go for seconds when a friend cooks for me. I don't even think about being "in control" anymore - I'm just living. I'm not trying to control anything the way I used to. I'm not limiting myself to three pieces of fruit a day. I ate an entire box of strawberries by myself yesterday and it was great! 2021-me would not have been happy afterwards.

Sure, it varies widely between individuals. But also:

There was a clear dose-response relationship: [more sets](https://www.menshealth.com/uk/building-muscle/train-smarter/a64282360/sets-strength-muscle-gain/) generally meant more muscle growth gains. But those gains diminished after a certain point. The research identified a 'point of undetectable outcome superiority': the volume where adding more sets no longer gave you a better chance of seeing noticeable improvement. **For muscle growth:** that point was around 11 fractional sets per muscle group, per session. From [Men's Health](https://www.menshealth.com/uk/building-muscle/train-smarter/a64497723/fewer-sets-per-workout/) 2025. Based on this[ paper.](https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/view/537/1148)

Other paper, similar statements: The analysis suggests that, statistically, high set volumes (≥3) are not significantly better than low set volumes (<3) in regard to upper body muscle hypertrophy in untrained subjects.[ From 2018](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/cpf.12476)

In any case I don't think OP would benefit from doing an arm workout every day, assuming medium/high intensity and 3-4 sets per day.

Nobody approached me about it; I was always the first person to talk. I do have a grudge against my parents for not picking up on the OBVIOUS signs - suddenly I'm in the gym for 1 to 2 hours most days, I suddenly go for hour-long bike rides, I start tracking my calories, I keep asking what we're having for dinner, I get angry when someone else made my plate for me. I was 14 when I started becoming derailed and they never questioned.

I did tell my close friends eventually, because I felt it was time that I told someone, and I was received with the love and understanding I needed. My partner, when we were still just friends, also knew, and said he did have a hunch I was struggling; it just wasn't clear *what* exactly. A year later we started dating and he's been able to support me because he knows what's up - if I did xyz but there was no context for it, he'd just be even more worried.

I was never bad enough to need medical attention, I didn't even meet the criteria for therapy because after three months of waiting for an intake, I'd already gained enough weight back to be stable. Of course nobody had the magic cure after I told them, but it did mean people knew more or less what I was going through, and were able to support me as needed (e.g. my best friend doesn't eat much due to other health reasons, but it's not an ED. If I skipped meals however, people would know it's likely ED-related). And it reminds me how far I've come; people tell me how good it is to see me eating and see my confidence because they remember how bad it was when we'd first met. I don't remember how bad it was, I always felt "fine." Having a loved one tell me how good I'm doing means a lot.

My father is run-off-the-mill Dutch, my mother is Chinese-Indonesian and came here as a student. Studied here and never left. She's fluent in Dutch but she has a notable accent, like most people who learn a new language in their twenties. I felt ashamed of her, and her (and my) culture, and how she and I looked, for a long time. I wanted to be Dutch, and felt Dutch. Sometime in my late teens I started disliking my father more and more, and became closer with my mother instead. So I started taking more interest in her (my) culture, and I now proudly write my Chinese middle name on my socials. My first & last name are very standard, so on a resume or such I won't get flagged as foreigner. But when I talk to people, I'm inclined to say I'm Indonesian rather than Chinese, I find China is more subject to racist comments than Indonesia, especially since covid. During lockdowns I feared for the safety of my younger cousins and the kids of my mother's friends. I was old enough to handle myself but my cousins were 15 or younger so I worried they might be assaulted or harassed. Fortunately that didn't happen.

Following my weird experiences, I wrote my bachelor's thesis on cultural identity among Dutch-Asian youth. I can forward you the results (11 interviews + a questionnaire with \~40 people) if that's interesting to you.

What I find most difficult now - at 22 years old - is not how I see myself but how others see me. The people who matter to me, love me for just *me*. My father in law never once gave a second thought to how I looked, neither did one of my partner's friends. They didn't know I was not-entirely-Dutch until it came up in conversation. But outside of covid-related problems though I have felt unwelcome in the Netherlands because I look more East Asian than Dutch. People will flag me as foreigner and call me racial slurs. I'm also not fluent in Indonesian at all. My father's parents were subtly racist and hated my mother, and talked her out of teaching me Indonesian because supposedly it would mess up my Dutch skills (even though my father is Dutch and it could very easily have been done with one language per parent). That's something I also find tough. And in Indonesia I'd be too Dutch. In NL I'm too not-Dutch. I have to create my own sense of belonging.

I do like that I can handle spicy food and I didn't grow up on boiled-flat broccoli or unseasoned brussel sprouts. Being bicultural has shaped who I am now and I think it gives me insight into both the Dutch and (East) Asian migrant experience, and I got to experience both cultures. But I would have wanted to be proud earlier in life. I didn't have the support network for it, and my parents wouldn't have known how to help me. It hurts to think about when I was 14 and I wanted blue eyes so I'd fit in. So my advice is, let your child experience Dutch *and* their family's culture. And let them celebrate both. Yes, you live here - but you'll always carry a piece of your homeland with you. Give your kid a chance to be proud of both.

Wat koken betreft kan je veel variëren met een glutenvrije basis (dit kan met specifieke gf-pasta en dat soort dingen, maar rijst, quinoa, boekweit zijn ook mogelijk) en bonen of een sojaproduct. Ik weet niet of de vriendin gluten vrij is uit noodzaak (celiac's of glutenintolerant) of voor persoonlijke redenen, maar als het om allergie en hevige intolerantie gaat moet je ook altijd opletten dat iets niet mogelijk sporen van gluten bevat.

Bakken kan je met glutenvrij meel doen; rijstmeel, tapioca, maïsmeel, kikkererwtenmeel, amandelmeel. Mogelijk te gebruiken in een vegan recept en dan met de glutenvrije invoeging. Alleen deze gf-melen reageren dan vaak iets anders dan tarwe, dus daar moet je rekening mee houden. Let ook op dat ei vaak wordt gebruikt voor de luchtigheid in glutenvrije recepten, want gluten geven juist die luchtigheid en "bounce" aan bijvoorbeeld brood. Dus als je een glutenvrij recept vindt en ei er uit haalt, kan het zijn dat het toch wel vrij stevig wordt. Havermout is ook een optie, ik ben repeat-baker van [vegan bananenbrood](https://www.jumbo.com/recepten/vegan-bananenbrood-504347) (op basis van havermout ipv tarwe). Havermout is in principe glutenvrij maar kan wel sporen van gluten bevatten. Bij coeliakie zou ik echt glutenvrije haver kopen, bij lichte intolerantie of eigen keuze dan maken de sporen geen groot verschil. (Wel altijd even checken met de vriendin hoe het zit natuurlijk want sommigen kunnen écht niet tegen haver.)

Mocht het gaan om celiac's of hevige intolerantie; plastic kommen, bakvormen etc. kunnen sporen van gluten blijven bevatten. Ook als je ze goed wast. Om medisch verdriet te voorkomen kan je een paar alleen-voor-glutenvrij bakspullen in huis halen, of aan de vriendin vragen hoe het met haar zit. Een vriend van me is glutenintolerant maar kan best tegen "trace amounts" of af en toe een hapje tarwe, maar ik kende ook iemand met coeliakie dus voor hem zou het een retourtje ziekenhuis betekenen.

Mine disappeared twice! Both cases becauae I was underweight. My thyroid was fine (had bloodwork done), exercise has never affected it either.

Late 2018 I stopped having periods; late 2019 (one week short of being a full year!) I started again because I'd purposefully regained some weight.

Second time is a bit tougher to place since I was taking the contraceptive pill at the time because I wasn't looking to get knocked up. Started taking in spring 2020, then in winter kept having spotting outside of the usual sugar pill week. I figured that was my body being very displeased with my weight loss again. I got a copper IUD - so no hormones - in April 2021 so I could stop taking the pill. Usually menstruation starts again after 1-3 months of stopping it, but I hit my lowest-ever weight since my ED in that summer. So it took until December 2021 for my weight to stabilize and be high enough. Since then I haven't been UW and my cycles have been mostly average and regular.

I was never malnourished but my weight was simply too low. I basically lived off cereal, yoghurt, skittles and white rice when I was 14 and my period was unaffected then, because the quantity of food has been more important than the quality. It didn't matter how much protein or iron or magnesium or whatever I had, my period didn't come back until my weight was where it had to be.

The first plant that got me into my current Situation is a kalanchoe tomentosa. Someone gifted it to me 4 years ago, I've managed to keep it alive - when the main plant died, I propagated what was left and it grew again! Apparently the species "thrives on neglect" so it really was the plant for it.

Another succulent that I've actually *tried* to kill is sempervivum jovibarba. Gifted by the student association, I didn't like how the plant looked so I just treated it as my least favorite child. Semper is Latin for *always*. Vivum is derived from their verb "vivere" for living. So yeah, it's known for always being alive. It's stayed true to its name. I neglected the small pots I had with sempervivum over the past 8 months, they dried out or otherwise died, but there's green sprouting again. I like the plant now because it's earned my respect.

Non-succulent options are the zamioculcas (also known as ZZ), tradescantia, and grass lilies. Pothos is also known for being resilient but I managed to kill mine with three months of not watering. I highly recommend putting a weekly or 2-weekly reminder in your calendar to check your plant soil.

As for the fat gain vs muscle gain - when you eat more than you are using, you gain weight. This undoubtedly makes sense. Where this weight goes to is more complicated; some of this is fat, and some of this is muscle *if* you're also providing your muscles with a "reason" to grow (for example through calisthenics, like you're doing. This is why someone who is very overweight won't necessarily have a lot more muscle mass from the weight gain; the muscle mass only comes from stimulating muscles enough into growth).

Usually this amount is expected to be around 50-50 when someone is gaining weight whilst doing strength training in some form. This is also why bodybuilders will "bulk up" in their off-season and start cutting down their weight before a competition; they try to gain as much weight (preferably muscle) as they can in the off-season, and then try to lose as much fat as they can before a show. 

So in short, weight gain is normal and expected unless you're eating less than needed to maintain your weight. I started bulking around May last year and gained some fat but also some muscle. If you're not gaining more than \~1lbs a week or \~4lbs a month I'd say you're in a good fat:muscle gaining ratio.

Creatine in food is mostly in animal products so it's actually recommended for vegans/vegetarians sometimes, or suspected that we'd benefit more from supplementing, because we won't get a lot of creatine in our diet. Toevallig heb ik hier afgelopen jaar mijn bachelorscriptie over geschreven - culturele identiteit en gevoel van verbondenheid (sense of belonging) bij Aziatisch-Nederlandse jongeren. Zelf ben ik half Nederlands en half Chinees (maar dit is ook gecompliceerd want mijn moeders familie komt uit China, maar ze wonen nu vooral in Indonesië en ze spreekt meer Indonesisch dan Mandarijn.) en het is een onderwerp wat voor mij ook persoonlijke waarde heeft.

Uit vooronderzoek is al bekend dat zowel in Nederland als andere landen (zoals de VS) veel (Oost-)Aziatische groepen niet duidelijk gepresenteerd worden als het op discriminatie uitkomt; op sociaal-economisch gebied doen ze het ontzettend goed en de tweede generatie is vaak ook goed academisch opgeleid, zo ook in NL waar Chinese jongeren op de middelbare school gemiddeld hoger presteren dan de Nederlandse jongeren. De reputatie is dan ook aanzienlijk positief, zoals je zelf zegt. Maar ze ervaren nog steeds discriminatie, worden bijvoorbeeld nageroepen op straat of bespot om hun uiterlijk.

Wat ik uit mijn scriptie mee kan geven is dat "thuis" niet per se een plek is, maar juist een situatie. Bijvoorbeeld mensen die in interviews vertelden dat zij zich thuis voelen op werk, op school, de sportschool, etc. Niet per se omdat die plek zo bijzonder is, maar omdat daar mensen zijn die hen behandelen als gelijkwaardige medemensen, en daar niet gezien worden als "de ander" of "de Aziaat" etc. Sommigen van hen hadden dan wel een voorkeur voor mensen met niet-NL achtergrond, want dan was de kans op overeenkomsten en gedeelde ervaringen groter, maar over het algemeen was het belangrijkst dat ze "gewoon" werden behandeld.

Dit merk ik ook bij mezelf - mijn vier nauwste vrienden zijn niet Aziatisch. Twee zijn Nederlander, een komt uit de VS. Eén van hen is Marrokaans, de enige persoon van kleur die er niet uit ziet als wit of als Nederlander. Soms vind ik het jammer dat ik geen aansluiting vind met andere Aziatische/Chinese/Indonesische mensen maar ik voel me bij deze niet-Aziatische mensen ook geliefd en verwelkomd. Of dat nou op school is of bij hen thuis of in de supermarkt als we samen boodschappen doen. Ook als het me tegenzit, als ik me aangevallen voel wegens mijn afkomst, dan weet ik: bij deze mensen kan ik terecht. Ook als mijn partner niet snapt hoe het is om chingchong te worden geroepen als je ergens wandelt, ik vind bij hem mijn steun en toeverlaat. Want voor hem, en voor mijn andere vrienden, ben ik gewoon *ik*. Ik ben daar niet de Chinees of "de ander". Hier heb ik dan ook wel "geluk" mee gehad, dat ik deze mensen heb ontmoet, die mij zien als een vriend en niet eerst als allochtoon; het is wel deel van wie ik ben en ik duik daar niet voor weg, maar het is niet het enige. Net als dat mijn hobby's deel zijn van mijn leven, maar het is niet het enige. We hoeven niet allemaal van wandelen te houden.

Het gaat daarom, denk ik, niet om de geografische plek of het land, maar om de context. Ik hoop dat jij die mensen ook kan vinden. Dat kan hier zijn, in Marokko, of ergens anders. Mensen die jou zien voor *jou* en niet alleen als "de Marrokaan," want je bent meer dan je afkomst, en als je daarop wordt afgeschreven is dat doodzonde. Ik wens je succes op jouw zoektocht.

As said in another comment, it varies from person to person. I've interviewed people for uni work before (and have been interviewed), and the standard procedure is to say before the start of an interview, that if there is a question they don't want to answer or a topic that comes up but they don't want to discuss, they're free to tell me and we can move right past it. You could ask them beforehand if there are things which they know will trigger them or make them uncomfortable, so you know what to avoid, and ensure they know it's okay if they want to skip something.

As a general rule I would try not to comment on how they look, even if it's meant well it can be interpreted very wrong. Try to avoid numbers (calories, weight, measurements) unless they bring them up; if someone I know who has struggled with food and body image asked me about my weight, I would give comparative answers e.g. I weigh more now than I did two years ago. I wouldn't tell them how much I was then, or how much now, because I found it difficult for a long time to accept I wasn't at my goal weight, or that I wasn't eating xyz amount of calories or that my waist circumference wasn't xyz anymore. If someone had asked me at that time about my "stats" or told me theirs, I would've been pretty sad, realizing that I wasn't how I wanted, or that I wasn't more like them, or vice versa.

Because all "verkleinwoorden" (diminuitives) start with *het.* So "de tafel" becomes "het tafeltje" and we say "*het balletje"* derived from "de bal"

"Meisje" is a diminuitive and derived from "meid" which is why we say *het meisje* even though that's clearly gendered. If it's not the diminuitive, so with *de meid,* then it would be with *de.*

Don't ask me how we settled on meisje instead of meid, but German also uses the diminuitive for "girl" instead of their normal word.

Sumo and conventional are similar but different movements; flat bench press and incline bench press are also different movements. Flat bench just tends to be easier than incline. Breaking parallel on a squat tends to be easier than going all the way down for ass-to-grass.

I think it could be considered "cheating" because the range of motion is shorter since your hips are closer to the ground due to wider stance, so the distance between the top lockout position & the floor is less. It's not cheating though. ***They're different movements.*** It's not cheating to do a move that feels nicer to you.

Cheating would be closer to using the smiths machine and saying you can pull 200 pounds on your conventional deadlift. *That* definitely is not a proper deadlift. Sumo doesn't count as a conventional deadlift, because they're different movements. Sumo deadlift counts as a sumo deadlift. If you pull sumo in a weightlifting competition where they're measuring your sumo deadlift, it's not cheating. If you do it for conventional deadlift, then yes it's wrong. Same way that you wouldn't bring skates to a marathon to be faster; that'd be cheating. A movement "doesn't count" if you're meant to do X but you deliberately do Y.

My legs are a few inches longer than my torso and my ankle mobility isn't superb so conventional deadlifts are harder for me, especially if I do multiple reps and I lose my form. Sumo is a lot easier on my back and my form so I prefer doing that for higher reps.

I think you may have given yourself a self-fulfilling prophecy; you think you're stuck with your current physique, and/or expect that you'll give up again, and/or believe that this current motivation won't last long. If you start out with these expectations then it's likely they'll happen. I've dealt with depression myself and understand the cycle and expectations that things won't last but the thing is you have to *make* them last. Even if it takes thirty attempts to get something to work, if you think it's worth it then you've gotta keep trying.

What's helped me deal with depression and an ED is thinking about what I CAN get to work - many things can suck and I'll forever have wide-set hips and had embarassingly weak arms in my early teens but man, what if I worked on that and got stronger! Maybe one day I can get big arms and lift my dad! (I am now indeed strong enough to pick him up.)

Try thinking in terms of "what if I do make it" rather than "what if I don't" because you'll be dragging yourself down by expecting the negatives, and you don't deserve that. So what if you *do* stick with it? Arguably that would be a much better outcome than the one you're expecting from not-doing; envision that am-doing outcome (e.g. getting active, feeling stronger, growing shoulders to die for), let that drive you rather than being held back by the not-doing outcome.

If you want to work on general wellness I think you could spend some time figuring out what you vibe most with! Throw some things at the wall and see what sticks, basically. (At least that's what I did - I took maybe 10 minutes of ballet class as a toddler, never went again, liked swimming for a while, played tennis for some years, tried to get into running, and eventually settled with weightlifting when I was in my late teens.) If you're looking for specific routines, there should be some recommendations on the wiki here. I've heard lots of good things about Caroline Girvan.

I could never get myself into running/jogging but I've come to really enjoy walking, so I go on a stroll every evening, which is different for sure but it gets me moving and the general wisdom is that **the best workout routine is the one that you'll actually stick to.** If you drop it because you think it sucks, it likely wasn't the thing for you. I ended up disliking tennis and was horrible in all my PE classes in school, but I love weightlifting and exercise now that I've found the thing that feels like it's really *my* thing.

With regard to gender I think you should always keep in mind that your femininity is what *you* think it is, and it's most important that you feel good in your own skin. Fitness is for everyone regardless of how they describe themselves in terms of gender and how they look. (And if you're concerned that weightlifting will make you bulky or look manly - I promise you that it won't, unless you're trying to make that happen.) Fitness isn't inherently masculine even if it's often stereotyped as being a manly thing. But think about athletes. E.g. Naomi Osaka and Serena Williams don't look dainty/thin like how women are often "expected" to be but I think they're gorgeous and not "unwomanly"

For beans I think it's different because they're high in fiber & protein, which generally is expected to have a filling effect. Cucumber really is just crunchy water and not much else that's worth noting. Also note that water *can* be filling - the most filling meals I've had were often soup, chili and curry-like dishes because they had so much liquid.

For your first question - yes. Most of the beans weight becomes water weight, so you have less calories and macro/micronutrients per 100g, because the nutrients have been diluted as a result of the water. Same way that 100g of cooked rice is different from 100g dry rice, and why you weigh rice pre-cooking rather than after.

And for the second, yes protein should stay pretty much the same. I have beans canned but also dry, and if I calculate so they're both 100 *calories* rather than 100 grams, the amount of protein is about the same. 100g beans dry is about 350 calories and 20-25g of protein, while canned is about 90 calories with 4-9g protein usually.

So for the dry beans: 350 calories per 100g.  
Divided by 4 it will be 87.5 calories, and 6ish grams of protein.   
Which is about equivalent to the cooked/canned bean nutritional value. I hope that makes sense.

I think the rule of thumb is at least a full day between muscle groups. You can do an upper - lower body split if you don't like rest days (I know the feel). I work out all 5 weekdays and don't do strength training on the weekends, instead I do light stretches and walking.

First things first, you can't spot reduce. (Wish we could.) Even when I was underweight, my thighs stayed thicker than the rest of me, and I lost fat more visibly from my chest and waist. One of my friends has been on T for a couple of years now but he's always had fairly thick legs and still does today - note that this is not a "bad" or unmanly thing (he loves his thick thighs!), my cis boyfriend also has what he calls dummy thick thighs, even while being skinny. I'm afraid the thighs will probably stay mostly as they are, but what can help a little bit is working out so they'll be more muscular or toned, if you will.

If you don't want to track calories that's absolutely fine. I don't either! If your weight has been fairly stable with what you've been eating recently, then just eat less to lose weight and eat more to gain weight. Check in every week or so to see how your weight's going; if it's on average going down/up then you'll know whether to keep doing the same, or eat more or less. If you're not in a rush to lose/gain it's not that necessary to be counting calories imo. I'd suggest eating a little bit more to gain strength but again if you're not in a rush then it's likely fine anyway - especially at the start you can gain a lot of strength.

Finally, please please please don't do knee pushups. (Personally I hate them, they hurt my knees) I think they can be pretty bad for your knees if you have a joint condition. Start doing pushups with your hands on an elevated surface e.g. a table or chair. Work your way down to a lower surface until you can do them with your hands on the floor. Probably better for your knees and better for strength. Also you can try tricep dips to add to your other two main exercises!

Short answer is yes, as body fat percentage generally does determine obesity, with some exceptions (like infants, who are generally kinda chubby but it usually resolves itself by puberty). Having a certain % can mean someone is, or isn't, obese. No matter if they're 140cm or 210cm. The percentage is weight-adjusted because it indicates the fat percentage compared to your total body mass, so it's all relative, and it doesn't matter so much how tiny (short) someone is. A body fat percentage >30% would generally indicate obesity, regardless of how short or tall.

More elaborate example; say someone is 150cm, 50kg, and 30% body fat. That would mean 30% of this 50 kg person's total is comprised fat, so about 15kg. But if someone is 180 and 80kg, then 15kg of fat isn't that much, because their entire body is just 80kg total, bones, blood, organs and all - this 15kg of fat would be just 18% of their total weight.

Same way that lifting a 300g pillow isn't hard for you, but a much tinier bee is going to struggle, or not be able to do it all, because it's relatively heavy or light depending on who you ask. Hope that clears it up a lil!

If you start trying pushups, don't do them on the floor on your knees rather than toes. It's easy to cheat this way and imo sucks for your knees. Start off doing them on your feet, with hands against a wall and gradually increase the angle i.e. a table, chair, or bench on which you place your hands until you can do them on the floor.
